stories.title: AmTrustRE Completes 360 Lexington Avenue Repositioning
stories.excerpt: AmTrustRE has completed a comprehensive modernization at 360 Lexington Ave. in Manhattan. Led by preeminent New York-based architecture firm MdeAS Architects, the project reimagines the 268,000-square-foot office building as a modern, hospitality-driven workplace. AmTrustRE acquired the property in late 2024. “360 Lexington Avenue is an exceptional asset in one of Manhattan’s most connected locations, just steps from Grand Central and at the center of Midtown’s business district,” said Jonathan Bennett, president of AmTrustRE. “Our goal was to build on that inherent strength through a thoughtful modernization that positions the property for the next generation of office users. MdeAS has been an excellent partner throughout the process, bringing a deep understanding of the building’s character and a clear vision for how to elevate it while respecting what makes the property distinctive.” Built in 1959 and originally designed by Schuman & Lichtenstein, 360 Lexington Avenue reflects the transitional mid-century modern style that emerged in the postwar period. MdeAS designed a new double-height storefront framed by large-scale, angular metal panels that twist upward toward the corner, creating a more distinctive street presence. The post AmTrustRE Completes 360 Lexington Avenue Repositioning appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: AmTrustRE completed modernization of 268k SF office tower at 360 Lexington Ave, Manhattan.
Building repositioned as 'hospitality-driven workplace' with new storefront and mid-century modern refresh.
Prime Midtown location near Grand Central; target is next-gen office tenants.
stories.summary: AmTrustRE has completed a comprehensive modernization of 360 Lexington Avenue, a 268,000-square-foot office building in Manhattan's Midtown business district, acquired in late 2024. The project, led by MdeAS Architects, reimagines the 1959 structure as a modern, hospitality-driven workplace with a new double-height storefront and angular metal paneling. The firm aims to position the asset for contemporary office users in one of Manhattan's most connected locations.
stories.impact: Office repositioning efforts signal lingering pressure on Manhattan office landlords to compete for tenants, but do not directly drive multifamily demand. However, a successful 'experiential workplace' play at a transit-rich Midtown location could stabilize office leasing and indirectly strengthen foot traffic and retail/restaurant ecosystems that attract working professionals to nearby residential neighborhoods—potentially benefiting multifamily demand in Midtown East/Roosevelt Island submarkets.

stories.title: Hudson Pacific Extends Maturity on $1.1B Hollywood Media Loan
stories.excerpt: Hudson Pacific Properties, Inc. and its joint venture partner have extended the $1.1-billion CMBS loan secured by the Hollywood Media Portfolio. The extension moves the loan’s maturity to Nov. 9, 2027, with the stated interest rate unchanged and no principal paydown required at closing. The 2.2-million-square-foot Hollywood Media Portfolio includes Sunset Gower Studios, Sunset Las Palmas Studios and Sunset Bronson Studios, along with five on-lot or adjacent Class A office properties, ICON, EPIC, Harlow, 6040 Sunset and CUE. The portfolio also includes rights to build another 1.1 million square feet of office and production space. Hudson Pacific owns a 51% interest in the portfolio through the JV and oversees day-to-day operations, leasing and development. “This extension underscores our ability to execute a positive outcome for shareholders,” said Harout Diramerian, Hudson Pacific’s CFO. “It provides us with additional time and flexibility to advance our leasing strategy across this portfolio, while proactively managing our broader debt maturity schedule. The post Hudson Pacific Extends Maturity on $1.1B Hollywood Media Loan appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Hudson Pacific extended $1.1B CMBS loan on Hollywood Media Portfolio to Nov. 2027, no principal paydown due.
Portfolio includes 2.2M SF studios, offices, plus 1.1M SF development rights in Los Angeles.
Extension provides leasing and debt-maturity flexibility; indicates lender support amid media/production sector uncertainty.
stories.summary: Hudson Pacific Properties and its joint venture partner extended a $1.1 billion CMBS loan backed by the Hollywood Media Portfolio to November 9, 2027, with no changes to the interest rate or mandatory principal reduction. The 2.2-million-square-foot portfolio comprises three major studios (Sunset Gower, Las Palmas, Bronson) and five adjacent Class A office properties, plus development rights for another 1.1 million square feet. Hudson Pacific holds a 51% stake and oversees operations and leasing.
stories.impact: Loan extension signals continued capital market support for media/entertainment real estate in Los Angeles despite sector headwinds, reducing near-term distress risk. This stability supports ongoing activity in Hollywood and adjacent submarkets, but the extension itself does not materially affect multifamily demand or supply; however, if the portfolio successfully leases new creative/production tenants, it could drive ancillary employment growth and residential demand in central Los Angeles submarkets near studio infrastructure.

stories.title: Friedman’s Restaurant Expands with Upper West Side Location
stories.excerpt: Lee & Associates NYC announced that the ownership group behind Friedman’s Restaurant, Pastrami Queen and many other successful restaurant concepts has acquired an approximately 5,000-square-foot retail cooperative unit at 541-555 Amsterdam Ave. on Manhattan’s Upper West Side for $4.135 million. Peter Braus, president of Lee NYC, represented the buyer, Mountain View Acquisition LLC. The seller, 176 West 87th Leasehold LLC, a family LLC, was represented by Brandon Polakoff and his team at Avison Young. Joshua Stein acted as the seller’s representative and counsel. The property is currently home to Barney Greengrass, the longtime Upper West Side restaurant and appetizing shop, and Hudson & Charles, a neighborhood butcher shop. Both businesses will remain in place following the sale. The new owners will occupy an existing vacant restaurant space at the property, where they plan to open a new Friedman’s Restaurant location tailored to appeal to the Upper West Side neighborhood. “The Group is expanding its footprint in a top location on the Upper West Side, while also keeping a New York institution intact and operating for years to come,” said Braus. The post Friedman’s Restaurant Expands with Upper West Side Location appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Friedman's Restaurant group acquired 5k SF retail coop at 541-555 Amsterdam Ave, Upper West Side, for $4.135M.
New Friedman's location to occupy vacant space; existing tenants Barney Greengrass and Hudson & Charles remain.
Retail consolidation and neighborhood expansion by established restaurant operator.
stories.summary: The ownership group behind Friedman's Restaurant and Pastrami Queen acquired approximately 5,000 square feet of retail space at 541-555 Amsterdam Avenue on Manhattan's Upper West Side for $4.135 million. The group plans to open a new Friedman's location in a vacant restaurant space within the property, while longtime tenants Barney Greengrass and Hudson & Charles will continue operating. The acquisition reflects continued neighborhood retail investment.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Retail tenancy stability on the Upper West Side (historic food/service establishments remaining; new casual dining entry) suggests neighborhood foot traffic and local demand resilience, but does not signal population in-migration, job growth, or rental demand drivers that would warrant new apartment development or influence underwriting.

stories.excerpt: “You’ll see requirements out in the market and [tenants] have 10 options, 15 options. So when we get a deal, we have to move fast. There’s a lot of urgency and anxiety on the landlord’s side to be able to get it done.” That’s Julian Freeman (pictured above), partner with Cox, Castle & Nicholson, on the opportunities and challenges he sees in the industrial market at present. In addition to Freeman, you”ll also hear from Ken Fields, partner, Greenberg Glusker; Joe Vargas, president, Wonderful Real Estate; Andry Bratt, principal, Gantry; and Eddie Prosser, COO, Thorofare Capital. The post Industry Experts on the Challenges, Opportunities in Western Industrial Market (VIDEO) appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Western industrial market panel discussion at Connect Industrial West 2026 in Irvine, California.
Expert commentary highlights tenant urgency and landlord competition; 10–15 options per deal typical.
Industry leaders cite leasing pressure and market velocity but provide no specific supply/demand metrics.
stories.summary: Industry experts discussing the Western U.S. industrial market at the Connect Industrial West 2026 conference reported a highly competitive leasing environment with tenants enjoying abundant options (10–15 per deal). Panelists, including Julian Freeman (Cox, Castle & Nicholson), Ken Fields (Greenberg Glusker), Joe Vargas (Wonderful Real Estate), and others, noted significant landlord anxiety and urgency to close deals but did not provide detailed data on supply, occupancy, or pricing.
stories.impact: Commentary reflects a well-supplied, tenant-favorable industrial market in the West, with no structural shortage driving new development urgency. For multifamily developers, this suggests limited population in-migration pressure tied to industrial employment (which typically supports warehouse/logistics jobs of lower wage profiles). No material signal for multifamily demand or supply pipeline in Western submarkets unless paired with high-wage office/tech growth.

stories.title: OPEN Impact Arranges Coney Island Ground Lease for Charter School
stories.excerpt: OPEN Impact Real Estate represented Coney Island Preparatory Public Charter School in securing a 39-year leasehold condominium for a new 45,190-square-foot ground-up high school at 773 Neptune Ave. in Brooklyn. The new facility will allow Coney Island Prep to expand its high school enrollment and create new specialty instructional spaces. The ground-up, build-to-suit facility at 773 Neptune Ave. will be occupied exclusively by Coney Island Prep. The new development is being constructed by Rybak Development. Occupancy is expected in summer 2027. The new campus will allow Coney Island Prep to grow to serve more than 500 high school students, relocating its existing high school from 294 Avenue T in Gravesend to Coney Island proper. OPEN’s brokerage team included Alexander Smith and Stephen Powers. The landlord, 773 Neptune Avenue Qoz LLC, owned by Elie Fouerti, represented itself in-house. The ground lease follows a 15-year lease for another charter school, Launch Expeditionary Learning Charter School, in Sunset Park. The post OPEN Impact Arranges Coney Island Ground Lease for Charter School appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Coney Island Prep secured 39-year ground lease for 45,190 SF build-to-suit high school at 773 Neptune Ave, Brooklyn.
Rybak Development constructing; occupancy summer 2027; school expects 500+ high school students.
Charter school expansion relocating from Gravesend; institutional anchor use in Coney Island proper.
stories.summary: OPEN Impact Real Estate arranged a 39-year leasehold condominium for Coney Island Preparatory Public Charter School to occupy a 45,190-square-foot build-to-suit high school at 773 Neptune Avenue in Coney Island, Brooklyn. Rybak Development is constructing the ground-up facility, with occupancy expected in summer 2027. The new campus will allow Coney Island Prep to expand enrollment to over 500 high school students, relocating from Avenue T in Gravesend to Coney Island proper.
stories.impact: Charter school expansion signals institutional confidence in Coney Island's trajectory and adds a stable, long-term anchor tenant that could support residential stabilization and minor foot-traffic growth in the immediate submarket. However, charter school serves a captive, tuition-free population and does not materially drive in-migration or rental demand by income-generating workers. The development does not affect multifamily supply pipeline but suggests local real estate activity and potential future zoning/institutional density interest.

stories.title: Azimuth Sells Bronx Educational Facility to Equality Charter School for $55M
stories.excerpt: Azimuth Development Group has handed over ownership of a school facility in the East Bronx that appears to have been a build-to-suit construction job for the firm. Azimuth President Guido Subotovsky signed a $54.5 million deed transfer of 801 Bartholdi Street to Equality Charter School, a tuition-free public school that will use the property as a 63,000-square-foot elementary school, according to property records. The property appears to have been completed in 2025 and contains two cafeterias, a gymnasium, and 6,000 square feet of recreational space on the rooftop. The site can accommodate 900 students, according to Azimuth’s website. It’s unclear who brokered the deal. Spokespeople for Azimuth and Equality Charter School did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Equality Charter School currently has an elementary school at 3901 White Plains Road, a middle school at 4140 Hutchinson River Parkway East, and a high school at 2141 Seward Avenue, all in the Bronx. It’s unclear if the school’s administration will be consolidating any of its existing facilities within the new Bartholdi Street location. Azimuth, founded in 2009 by Subotovsky, specializes in projects that benefit local communities such as the development of affordable housing as well as market-rate units. The company says it has built over 1 million square feet of mixed-use developments in the five boroughs since it was founded. In terms of educational facilities, Azimuth has previously teamed up with Joy Construction in the $140 million mixed-income development of two buildings and 330 rental units 2069 Bruckner Boulevard. It leased 12,000 square feet in that development to The Village School in June 2025. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Azimuth Development sold East Bronx school facility (801 Bartholdi St) to Equality Charter School for $54.5M.
63k SF elementary school completed 2025; 900-student capacity with gyms, cafeterias, rooftop recreation.
Charter school consolidation play; unclear if existing Equality sites will merge into new facility.
stories.summary: Azimuth Development Group transferred ownership of an 801 Bartholdi Street educational facility in the East Bronx to Equality Charter School for $54.5 million. The 63,000-square-foot property, completed in 2025, includes two cafeterias, a gymnasium, and 6,000 square feet of rooftop recreational space, with capacity for 900 students. Equality Charter School operates additional elementary, middle, and high school sites elsewhere in the Bronx and may consolidate operations at the new location.
stories.impact: Institutional real estate turnover in the Bronx signals active charter school development and possible facility consolidation, but does not directly impact multifamily demand or supply. If Equality consolidates multiple school sites into the new Bartholdi location, it could free up other Bronx properties for alternative redevelopment (residential, mixed-use), indirectly expanding the land pipeline; however, no signal of employment growth or population in-migration to warrant new apartment starts.

stories.title: Arc Capital Lands $29M Refi for Chapman Market in L.A.’s Koreatown
stories.excerpt: Arc Capital Partners has secured $29.3 million to refinance the Chapman Market, a nearly century-old retail and dining destination in Los Angeles’ Koreatown. Voya Investment Management provided the financing for the popular 41,241-square-foot property at 3465 West Sixth Street, also known as Chapman Plaza, along one of Koreatown’s primary commercial corridors. Arc Capital acquired the historic asset 10 years ago for $30 million, records show, and secured a $25.5 million bridge loan in 2021. The property opened in 1928 and was one of the first markets in the Western U.S. designed around the use of the automobile, according to the nonprofit L.A. Conservancy. It was designated as a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument. Chapman Market has evolved into a multi-tenant dining, retail and entertainment center with a heavy concentration of Korean food and specialty concepts. Tenants include Escala, Quarters Korean BBQ, KazuNori, Starbucks, Origin Korean BBQ, Shibuyala, Toebang Café, Danbi, Tiger Sugar Boba, BHC Chicken and Uncle Tetsu, along with private club Club HUE. Northmarq’s Joe Giordani, Alex Kane and Karl Weidell facilitated the debt along with Bryan Ley and Tim Kuruzar. “If you’ve been to this property, you know it sits at the epicenter of Koreatown’s vibrant nightlife,” Giordani said in a statement. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Arc Capital secured $29.3M refinance for Chapman Market, 41k SF retail/dining asset in L.A. Koreatown.
1928-built property (Chapman Plaza) designated L.A. Historic-Cultural Monument; multi-tenant Asian dining/retail hub.
Arc acquired 10 years ago for $30M; refi suggests stable tenant base and neighborhood anchoring.
stories.summary: Arc Capital Partners refinanced the Chapman Market (Chapman Plaza), a 41,241-square-foot retail and dining destination in Los Angeles' Koreatown, with $29.3 million in long-term financing from Voya Investment Management. The property, built in 1928 and designated as a Los Angeles Historic-Cultural Monument, is now a multi-tenant Korean food, specialty retail, and entertainment center with tenants including KazuNori, Quarters Korean BBQ, Origin, Starbucks, and Club HUE. Arc acquired the asset 10 years ago for $30 million and had secured a $25.5 million bridge in 2021.
stories.impact: Successful refinance of a historic, tenant-dense retail landmark in Koreatown indicates stable, community-anchored retail demand in Los Angeles' ethnic commercial corridor. This supports neighborhood stability and foot traffic but does not signal major residential in-migration or job growth. Koreatown's continued vitality as a dining/cultural hub could sustain moderate multifamily demand among service workers and young professionals, but the deal itself does not meaningfully affect apartment supply pipeline or rent growth drivers.

stories.title: In Health Care Real Estate, Creativity Abounds — It Has To
stories.excerpt: Health care is an ever-evolving entity, from the way patients are treated to where they are treated. In addition to the twin challenges of providing quality care and turning a profit while doing so, health systems are navigating regulatory pressure, accelerated project timelines and other real estate issues. On Thursday, Sept. 10, Commercial Observer gathered together capital planning executives, legal experts, construction managers and project leaders at its National Healthcare Forum, which was hosted in the Proshansky Auditorium of the City University of New York Graduate Center. During the event, experts discussed what it takes to shape the next iteration of health care infrastructure through strategies such as rethinking how funds are allocated to the best practices for revitalizing aging facilities. The day kicked off with a conversation between Vincent Grippo, senior vice president of real estate and facilities services at Northwell Health, and Mitch Green, senior vice president with AECOM Tishman. Mitch Green and Vincent Grippo. PHOTO: Greg Morris/For Commercial Observer Grippo began by sharing his story, which includes a 25-year career across several client-facing organizations. Most poignantly, Grippo shared that he is seven years cancer free — a cancer developed due to exposure to toxic air caused by the 9/11 terrorist attacks. With that revelation, Grippo requested a moment of silence to honor those who had been and are still being impacted by that morning 25 years ago Friday. As the conversation got underway, Grippo and Green focused on the best strategies and the challenges to funding and improving aging infrastructure investments across hospital systems. bullets: Commercial Observer National Healthcare Forum convened experts on health care real estate strategy and innovation.
Panel included Northwell Health SVP of Real Estate and AECOM Tishman SVP; topics: project timelines, capital allocation, aging facility revitalization.
Forum highlighted regulatory pressure and accelerated timelines as industry challenges.
stories.summary: Commercial Observer hosted its National Healthcare Forum at CUNY Graduate Center, gathering capital planning executives, legal experts, construction managers, and project leaders to discuss health care real estate strategy. Key panelists included Vincent Grippo (Northwell Health, SVP Real Estate & Facilities) and Mitch Green (AECOM Tishman, SVP). The forum addressed fund allocation strategies, best practices for aging facility revitalization, regulatory pressures, and accelerated project timelines within health care development.
stories.impact: Healthcare sector panel discussion signals ongoing capital reallocation toward modernization and adaptive reuse of aging medical facilities, but does not provide specific market metrics or project data relevant to multifamily. No visible link to residential demand or supply; however, if major health systems accelerate campus expansion or recruitment (e.g., Northwell in NYC suburbs), it could indirectly drive employment and housing demand in secondary markets near major medical centers.

stories.title: Andreessen Horowitz to Open West Palm Office for Defense-Tech Bets
stories.excerpt: Venture capitalist behemoth Andreessen Horowitz is opening an office in West Palm Beach, Fla., which will focus on defense-tech investments. The firm, also known as a16z, signed a lease at Related Ross’ CityPlace Tower, according to a representative for the landlord, who declined to provide the size of the footprint. The office, which is scheduled to open early next year, will serve as a regional headquarters for a16z’s $1.18 billion American Dynamism fund, led by general partner Katherine Boyle, the Menlo Park, Calif.,-based firm announced. A representative for a16z did not immediately respond to a request for additional details. The transaction marks another West Palm Beach win for Stephen Ross, Related Ross’ billionaire owner, who has launched a $10 billion development spree to turn the city into a leading tech and finance hub. Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Chase have all signed leases at Related Ross-owned office buildings since the onset of the pandemic. The lease also marks a return to South Florida for a16z. In 2022, the firm opened an office in Miami Beach to make crypto investments, only to shutter the 8,300-square-foot base two years later — and three years before the end of agreement. A16z follows another defense-tech giant, Palantir, which relocated its global headquarters from Denver to Aventura this year. Ross purchased CityPlace Tower, where a16z will be based, for $175 million in 2021, according to property records. Built in 2008 at 525 Okeechobee Boulevard, the 18-story building spans 303,519 square feet. The developer is building two more Class A office buildings after obtaining a $772 million construction package last year. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Andreessen Horowitz leasing office at Related Ross' CityPlace Tower in West Palm Beach, Florida.
a16z $1.18B American Dynamism defense-tech fund establishing regional HQ; opening early 2026.
Follows Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan Chase leases; part of Ross' $10B tech/finance hub push.
stories.summary: Venture capital giant Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) signed a lease at Related Ross' CityPlace Tower in West Palm Beach, Florida, to open a regional headquarters for its $1.18 billion American Dynamism defense-tech fund, led by partner Katherine Boyle. The office is scheduled to open in early 2026. The transaction is part of a broader trend of major financial and tech firms (Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs, J.P. Morgan Chase) leasing space in West Palm Beach as billionaire Stephen Ross executes a $10 billion redevelopment initiative to position the city as a leading tech and finance hub.
stories.impact: a16z's West Palm Beach office opening signals executive-level and capital-markets migration to South Florida, driven by Ross's directed development strategy. This concentration of venture, defense-tech, and financial services talent will likely attract secondary corporate relocations, high-wage workers, and ancillary service professionals to West Palm Beach and surrounding South Florida markets (Boca Raton, Fort Lauderdale), materially strengthening multifamily rental demand and justifying new Class A apartment development in and around the central business district; cap rates may compress and rents rise in premium West Palm Beach/greater Miami submarkets over next 2–3 years.

stories.title: Longpoint Buys Miami-Dade Warehouse Portfolio for $195M
stories.excerpt: Longpoint Partners has dropped $195 million on a 10-building industrial portfolio in Miami-Dade County, the Boston-based private equity firm announced. The portfolio, composed of small-bay properties, spans 729,901 square feet across 41 acres. The buildings average about 73,000 square feet with clear heights ranging from 17 to 25 feet. They’re 90 percent leased to 74 tenants, each occupying an average 10,000 square feet. “This acquisition reflects the conviction and discipline that have guided our work here: acquiring functional, well-located small-bay industrial assets with a diverse tenant base in locations where new supply is difficult to create,” Dwight Angelini, co-founder and managing partner of Longpoint, said in a statement. A representative for Longpoint has yet to provide the addresses of the properties or the name of the seller. Since 2023, Longpoint Partners has been making sizable, bulk purchases of South Florida industrial properties. It has spent nearly $600 million on 51 buildings in two portfolio acquisitions. More recently in July, the firm bought three fully leased warehouses, totaling 121,579 square feet, for $39 million. Longpoint Partners also specializes in grocery-anchored retail properties. In June, it sold a 71,191-square-foot asset near Boynton Beach to Publix for $24 million. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Longpoint Partners acquired 10-building industrial portfolio in Miami-Dade County for $195M.
729,901 SF across 41 acres; 90% leased to 74 tenants; avg 73k SF/building, 17–25 ft clear heights.
Longpoint conviction play on small-bay, hard-to-replicate assets; part of $600M+ South Florida industrial spree since 2023.
stories.summary: Boston-based private equity firm Longpoint Partners acquired a 10-building industrial portfolio in Miami-Dade County for $195 million, comprising 729,901 square feet across 41 acres. The properties are small-bay assets averaging approximately 73,000 square feet per building with clear heights of 17 to 25 feet, currently 90% leased to a diverse tenant base of 74 operators averaging 10,000 square feet each. Since 2023, Longpoint has invested nearly $600 million in bulk purchases of South Florida industrial properties, acquiring 51 buildings across two transactions.
stories.impact: Aggressive institutional capital deployment into Miami-Dade small-bay industrial reflects supply scarcity and structural barriers to new development (land constraints, zoning, environmental); Longpoint's $600M+ South Florida footprint suggests confidence in port-adjacent logistics and last-mile demand growth. This signals sustained, high-wage distribution and logistics employment anchoring South Florida, which indirectly supports multifamily demand among blue-collar and logistics-adjacent workers. However, industrial acquisitions do not directly expand residential supply; developers should monitor Miami-Dade multifamily pipeline to ensure new apartment starts keep pace with employment, particularly in affordable/workforce segments supporting warehouse/logistics labor.
